White asked how to tell whether the best of many forecasting models or trading rules is genuinely better than a simple benchmark, or merely the luckiest of the batch. When the same data are searched repeatedly, the top performer's results are inflated by chance, a problem known as data snooping. His Reality Check tests the null hypothesis that none of the models considered beats the benchmark. For each model k it computes the average performance advantage over the benchmark, f_k; the test statistic is V = max over k of sqrt(n) * f_k, and its distribution under the null is obtained by resampling the data with a stationary bootstrap that preserves short-term dependence. Rule: judge the winning strategy against the distribution of the best result one would expect from the whole set of strategies tried, not against a single-test threshold, so the p-value accounts for every model searched. He illustrated the method with a large set of forecasting models for stock index returns, and it was soon applied to technical trading rules by Sullivan, Timmermann and White (1999). Caveat: the test needs a record of every model tried, and Hansen (2005) showed that including many poor or irrelevant models makes it overly conservative, proposing the Superior Predictive Ability test instead; stepwise methods by Romano and Wolf identify which individual models outperform.

West (1987), Econometrica 55(3), 703-708 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.2307/1913610 | Topics: linear regression; hypothesis testing

Newey and West asked how to compute reliable standard errors for regression estimates when the errors are both heteroskedastic (their variance changes over time) and autocorrelated (correlated with nearby errors), as happens with overlapping multi-period returns or persistent economic data. Ordinary least-squares standard errors assume neither problem and can then be far too small, making weak results look significant. Earlier corrections that simply summed estimated autocovariances could produce a negative variance, which is meaningless. Their estimator weights the autocovariances so that the result is always positive semi-definite. In words: the long-run variance S = Gamma_0 + the sum over lags j = 1 to L of (1 - j / (L + 1)) * (Gamma_j + Gamma_j'), where Gamma_j is the estimated covariance between terms j periods apart and the declining Bartlett weights 1 - j / (L + 1) shrink the more distant lags. The estimator is consistent when the lag window L grows slowly with the sample size. Standard errors computed this way, known as HAC (heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent) or simply Newey-West standard errors, became a default in empirical finance, including in Fama-MacBeth and return-predictability regressions. Caveat: results depend on the chosen lag length, which later work by Andrews (1991) and by Newey and West (1994) made data-driven, and in small samples with highly persistent regressors the standard errors are still too small, so tests reject too often.

Ljung and Box asked how to check, with a single number, whether a time series, or the residuals of a fitted model, still contain autocorrelation. Box and Pierce (1970) had proposed adding up the squared sample autocorrelations over the first h lags, but in samples of realistic size that statistic tended to come out too small, so it missed real dependence. Ljung and Box corrected each term for the number of observations behind it: Q = n * (n + 2) * the sum over k = 1 to h of r_k^2 / (n - k), where n is the sample size and r_k the lag-k sample autocorrelation. If the series is white noise, Q approximately follows a chi-squared distribution with h degrees of freedom (reduced by the number of estimated ARMA parameters when testing residuals), and their simulations showed this approximation is much closer than the one for the earlier statistic. In finance the test is applied to returns to look for predictability, which would contradict a random walk, and to squared returns to look for volatility clustering. Caveat: the chi-squared reference assumes independent observations under the null; with volatility clustering, as in most return series, the test rejects too often unless a robust version is used, and the answer can depend on the number of lags h chosen.

Jarque and Bera asked for a simple and powerful test of whether observations, or the residuals of a regression, come from a normal distribution. Working within the broad Pearson family of distributions, they derived a Lagrange multiplier test that depends only on the sample skewness S and kurtosis K: JB = (n / 6) * (S^2 + (K - 3)^2 / 4). A normal distribution has skewness 0 and kurtosis 3, so large values of JB signal departures from normality; under normality JB is approximately chi-squared with two degrees of freedom, so the 5 percent critical value is about 5.99. Their simulations showed the test had good power against a range of non-normal alternatives compared with other common tests. The test first appeared in a short 1980 note by the same authors in Economics Letters; the 1987 paper gives the full derivation and evidence. In finance it is routinely applied to returns and nearly always rejects normality for daily data because of fat tails. Caveat: the chi-squared approximation is poor in small samples, so exact or simulated critical values are needed; sample skewness and kurtosis are very sensitive to a few outliers; and a rejection says only that the data are not normal, not which distribution to use instead.

Dickey and Fuller asked how to test whether a time series has a unit root, meaning it behaves like a random walk whose shocks never fade, or is stationary, meaning it tends to return to a mean. In the model y_t = rho * y_(t-1) + e_t, a unit root means rho = 1, while rho below 1 implies mean reversion. Equivalently, one regresses the change, Delta y_t = (rho - 1) * y_(t-1) + e_t, and asks whether the coefficient on the lagged level is zero. The difficulty is that under the unit-root null the usual t-statistic does not follow Student's t distribution, so standard tables reject too often. Dickey and Fuller derived the correct limiting distributions of the estimator and its t-statistic, for models without a constant, with a constant, and with a constant and a time trend, and provided critical values computed by simulation. Rule: reject a unit root only when the t-statistic is more negative than the Dickey-Fuller critical value, about -2.86 at 5 percent when a constant is included, rather than the familiar normal value of -1.65. The augmented version, which adds lagged changes to absorb short-run correlation, followed in later work. In finance the test is used on spreads and prices to check for mean reversion, for example in pairs trading. Caveat: it has low power against slow mean reversion in short samples, and structural breaks can make a stationary series look like a random walk (Perron, 1989).

Poterba and Summers asked whether stock prices contain transitory components, temporary deviations from fundamental value that eventually reverse, and why such components would be hard to detect. They first showed that standard tests have little statistical power: a sizeable but slowly fading component could hide in return data for decades. They then applied variance-ratio tests to long histories of U.S. stock returns and to data from 17 other countries. Under a random walk the variance of k-period returns equals k times the one-period variance; they found returns positively autocorrelated over short horizons and negatively autocorrelated over horizons of several years, the signature of mean reversion. Their estimates implied that transitory components account for a large share of return variance, and they argued that changes in required returns driven by risk would struggle to explain such swings, pointing instead to slowly decaying price fads. Rule: variance ratio = Var(k-period return) / (k * Var(1-period return)); values below 1 at long horizons indicate mean reversion. Caveat: the evidence is statistically weak and leans heavily on the 1926-1946 period, which includes the Great Depression; Kim, Nelson and Startz found little mean reversion after 1946, and small-sample biases in long-horizon tests can create the appearance of reversion where none exists.

Jegadeesh asked whether monthly returns on individual U.S. stocks can be predicted from their own past returns. Using data from the 1930s to the 1980s, he estimated how each stock's return relates to its returns in previous months and then formed portfolios based on the predicted returns. He found a strong negative relation between a stock's return in one month and its return in the next, known as short-term reversal, and a positive relation with returns about a year earlier, a pattern that foreshadowed the momentum effect. Portfolios of the stocks with the highest predicted returns beat those with the lowest by a wide and statistically significant margin, which rejected the hypothesis that individual stock prices follow random walks. Rule: in a regression of this month's return on the returns of each of the previous twelve months, the lag-1 coefficient is negative and the lag-12 coefficient positive; so last month's biggest losers tend to outperform next month, and ranking stocks by prior one-month return and taking the opposite side earns a spread. The paper helped establish that predictability in individual stocks differs by horizon: reversal over a month, continuation over a year. Caveat: later work showed that much of the one-month reversal reflects bid-ask bounce, illiquidity and short-lived price pressure, so it shrinks sharply after trading costs and is much weaker among large, liquid stocks.

Uhlenbeck and Ornstein, two physicists, asked how the velocity and position of a small particle jostled by molecules (Brownian motion) evolve over time once friction is taken into account. Einstein's earlier theory treated the particle's displacement as a pure random walk; they modelled its velocity as being continually pulled back toward zero by friction while receiving random kicks. In the notation finance later adopted, the process is dX = theta * (mu - X) * dt + sigma * dW: over a short interval, X moves back toward its long-run mean mu at a speed proportional to its distance from it, plus a random shock. Its key properties: deviations decay exponentially on average, with a half-life of ln(2) / theta; the process settles into a stationary normal distribution with variance sigma^2 / (2 * theta); and the correlation between values decays exponentially with the time between them. Over long times the particle's position still spreads out like a random walk. Finance borrowed this Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as the standard model of mean reversion, for interest rates (Vasicek, 1977), commodity prices and the spreads between related securities in pairs trading. Caveat: applying it to markets assumes a constant mean and speed of reversion; in finite samples the estimated speed is biased upward, so mean reversion can look stronger than it is, and real spreads can stop reverting when the economic link between assets breaks.

Jegadeesh and Titman asked whether investors could profit by buying the stocks that had risen most over the past several months and selling those that had fallen most, in contrast with earlier studies that emphasised reversals over very short and very long horizons. Each month they ranked U.S. stocks by their returns over the previous 3 to 12 months, bought the top tenth and sold the bottom tenth, and held the positions for 3 to 12 months, overlapping portfolios formed in different months. Over 1965 to 1989 these strategies earned significant positive returns, and the profits were not explained by the stocks' market risk or by delayed reactions to common factors. Part of the gain reversed over the following two years, which they read as evidence of a delayed price response to firm-specific information rather than compensation for risk. Returns around subsequent earnings announcements showed a similar pattern. Rule: momentum return = return of the top tenth of stocks ranked by past 3-to-12-month return - return of the bottom tenth, with positions held for months rather than days. The finding became one of the most widely replicated anomalies, documented in many countries and asset classes. Caveat: high turnover means trading costs eat into momentum profits, and the strategy is prone to sudden severe crashes, especially when markets rebound sharply after a fall.

Carhart (1997), Journal of Finance 52(1), 57-82 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1997.tb03808.x | Topics: linear regression; momentum; Fama-French three-factor; factor model

Carhart asked whether mutual funds that did well in one year keep doing well, as earlier studies had suggested, and whether that persistence reflects managers' skill. He built a database of funds from 1962 to 1993 that includes funds that later closed or merged, avoiding survivor bias. To measure performance he extended the Fama-French three-factor model with a fourth factor for one-year stock momentum: fund return - risk-free rate = alpha + b * market excess return + s * SMB + h * HML + p * momentum + error, where SMB is small-minus-big, HML is high-minus-low book-to-market and the momentum factor is past-year winners minus losers. He found that the apparent persistence among top funds is largely explained by their exposure to momentum stocks, often simply from holding last year's winners, and by differences in expenses and trading costs, not by stock-picking skill. The one robust persistence was at the bottom: the worst funds tended to stay poor. His four-factor model became a standard benchmark for evaluating fund managers and equity strategies. Caveat: the factors are empirical choices rather than consequences of a theory, and later evidence, such as bootstrap studies of fund alphas, suggests that a small number of managers may have genuine skill even though the average fund does not.

Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen asked whether an asset's own past return predicts its future return, as distinct from the usual cross-sectional momentum that compares assets with one another. Studying 58 liquid futures and forward contracts on equity indexes, currencies, commodities and government bonds over several decades, they found that an asset's excess return over the past 12 months positively predicted its return in the following month, with the effect lasting up to about a year and partly reversing afterwards. They called this time series momentum. A diversified strategy that goes long each contract whose past-year return was positive and short each whose return was negative, with every position scaled to the same target volatility, earned substantial returns with little exposure to standard asset-pricing factors, and did especially well during extreme market moves, including 2008. Rule: position = sign(past 12-month excess return) * (target volatility / estimated volatility of the asset). They linked the pattern to initial under-reaction followed by delayed over-reaction, and used futures-market position data to show that speculators tend to ride the trends while hedgers take the other side. Caveat: later studies argued that the evidence of predictability for individual assets is weaker than the pooled results suggest and that much of the strategy's performance comes from the volatility scaling, and trend-following funds went through a long weak stretch in the 2010s.

Moskowitz (2016), Journal of Financial Economics 122(2), 221-247 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2015.12.002 | Topics: momentum; volatility targeting

Daniel and Moskowitz asked when momentum strategies suffer their rare but devastating losses, and whether those losses can be anticipated. Studying U.S. equities back to 1927 as well as other markets and asset classes, they found that momentum crashes happen in panic states: after a prolonged market decline, while volatility is high, and at the moment the market rebounds sharply, as in 1932 and 2009. The mechanism is that after a fall the loser portfolio is full of beaten-down, high-beta stocks, so a long-winners, short-losers position is effectively short the market; when the market jumps, the losers jump most and the strategy loses heavily. In these states its payoff resembles that of a short call option on the market. Because both the bear-market condition and high volatility can be observed in advance, the authors built a dynamic strategy that scales the momentum position each month by its forecast mean divided by its forecast variance, cutting exposure in panic states and adding it in calm ones. Rule: weight on momentum = c * (forecast momentum return / forecast momentum variance), with the constant c setting overall risk. This substantially raised the Sharpe ratio relative to static momentum, with similar results across markets. Caveat: the forecasts of momentum's mean rest on a modest number of crash episodes, gains are smaller after trading costs and real-time estimation, and a simpler rule that scales by momentum's own recent volatility (Barroso and Santa-Clara, 2015) captures much of the benefit.

Basu asked whether a stock's price-earnings (P/E) ratio, a piece of public information, could be used to earn returns beyond those justified by risk, which would contradict the semi-strong form of market efficiency. Using NYSE industrial firms from 1957 to 1971, he formed portfolios each year by ranking stocks on their P/E ratios and tracked their later performance. The low-P/E portfolios earned higher average returns than the high-P/E portfolios, and the difference remained after adjusting for risk with capital asset pricing model measures such as Jensen's alpha and the Sharpe and Treynor ratios. He also considered whether transaction costs, search costs and taxes would remove the advantage, concluding that a gap probably remained for some investors. Rule behind the value idea: stocks priced cheaply relative to their earnings (low P/E, or equivalently a high earnings yield, E/P = 1 / (P/E)) have tended to outperform expensive ones on average. He interpreted the result as evidence that the information in P/E ratios was not fully reflected in prices. Caveat: low-P/E stocks also tend to be smaller and more distressed, so later studies debated whether the effect is separate from the size effect; Fama and French (1992) found that book-to-market captures much of it; whether the premium compensates for risk or reflects mispricing is still contested; and value premiums were notably weak in the 2010s.

Banz asked whether a firm's size, measured by the market value of its common stock, helps explain average stock returns once risk is accounted for with the capital asset pricing model. Using NYSE common stocks from 1936 to 1975, he estimated a model in which expected return depends on beta and on the firm's relative market value. Smaller firms had, on average, higher risk-adjusted returns than larger firms, which became known as the size effect, and the effect had been present for at least forty years. It was not linear: it was concentrated among the very smallest firms, with little difference between average-sized and large firms. Rule: expected return = risk-free rate + beta * market premium + an extra term that is larger the smaller the firm's market value, so in that sample small capitalisation predicted higher returns. Banz was careful to say he could not tell whether size itself mattered or whether it stood in for some unknown factor correlated with size, but he concluded that the result was evidence the CAPM was misspecified. Caveat: the size premium largely faded after the early 1980s, has been concentrated in the smallest and least liquid stocks and in January, and later work argues that much of it reflects illiquidity or poor-quality firms; it shows up more reliably when firm quality is controlled for.

Fama and French asked which characteristics of stocks actually explain why some earn higher average returns than others, putting the capital asset pricing model's beta in a contest with size, earnings yield, leverage and the book-to-market ratio. Using NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ stocks from 1963 to 1990, they estimated betas carefully, forming portfolios on both size and pre-ranking beta so that beta's effect could be separated from size's, and ran Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions of monthly returns on the characteristics. Once size was controlled for, beta showed essentially no relation to average return. Two easily measured variables, market equity (size) and the ratio of book equity to market equity, together captured the cross-sectional variation in average returns and absorbed the roles of leverage and earnings yield: small stocks and stocks with high book-to-market (value stocks) earned higher average returns. Rule: in monthly regressions return_i = c0 + c1 * ln(size_i) + c2 * ln(book-to-market_i) + error, the average c1 was negative and c2 positive, while beta added nothing. They suggested these variables might proxy for risk, perhaps related to financial distress. Caveat: critics argued the results could reflect data-snooping or survivorship bias in accounting data, that beta's relation to returns reappears with longer samples or annual returns, and whether the value and size premiums reward risk or reflect mispricing remains disputed.

Fama and French asked whether a few common risk factors could explain the returns on stocks and bonds over time, following their finding that size and book-to-market predict average stock returns. They built factor-mimicking portfolios: SMB (small minus big), the return on small-company stocks minus that on large-company stocks, and HML (high minus low), the return on high book-to-market (value) stocks minus low book-to-market (growth) stocks, alongside the stock market's excess return; for bonds they added TERM (long-term minus short-term government bonds) and DEF (corporate minus government bonds). In time-series regressions on 25 portfolios sorted by size and book-to-market, the three stock factors explained most of the variation in returns, often with R-squared above 0.9, and left intercepts close to zero, meaning the model largely captured the differences in average returns. Rule (three-factor model): excess return = alpha + b * (market return - risk-free rate) + s * SMB + h * HML + error, with alpha near zero when the model prices the asset correctly. The bond factors captured common variation in bond returns, and stock returns were linked to bond returns through those shared bond-market factors. The model became the standard benchmark for measuring abnormal returns. Caveat: it fails to explain momentum and later-documented patterns related to profitability and investment, which led to four- and five-factor models, and whether SMB and HML are true risk factors or labels for mispricing remains debated.

Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny asked why value strategies, which buy stocks with low prices relative to earnings, cash flow or book value, or with low past sales growth, had outperformed glamour stocks, and whether the extra return was simply compensation for risk. Using U.S. stocks from the late 1960s to around 1990, they confirmed that value portfolios earned substantially higher returns, with the strongest results when two measures were combined, such as a low price-to-cash-flow ratio and low past sales growth. They then tested the risk explanation directly: value stocks did not underperform in the states of the world where risk should hurt, such as falling markets and recessions, and if anything did relatively well. Their explanation was behavioural: investors extrapolate past growth too far into the future, overpaying for firms that have grown fast and underpricing firms that have done poorly, while the later growth of the two groups turned out much closer than prices had implied. Rule: rank stocks on ratios such as cash flow / price or book value / market value and on past sales growth, then buy the cheap, slow-growth group and avoid the expensive, fast-growth group whose prices embed over-optimistic extrapolation. Caveat: Fama and French countered that value stocks carry distress risk that these tests miss, the risk-versus-mispricing debate is unresolved, and value strategies suffered a long and deep drawdown in the 2010s, so the premium is far from guaranteed.

Haugen and Heins asked whether riskier stocks and portfolios have actually earned higher returns, as the theory of a positive risk-return trade-off predicts. Using several decades of U.S. stock data up to the early 1970s, they formed portfolios with different levels of risk, measured by the variance of monthly returns and by beta, and compared their realised average returns. They found no support for the idea that the market rewarded bearing this risk: over the long run, portfolios with lower variance earned average returns at least as high as, and often higher than, their riskier counterparts. Since a positive risk premium is central to both portfolio theory and the capital asset pricing model, they argued that this conventional assumption deserved rethinking. Rule of the low-volatility anomaly: theory says average return should rise with risk, but across stock portfolios the slope of average return on volatility or beta has been about zero or negative. The paper drew limited attention for many years but anticipated the later literature on low-risk investing, and Haugen went on to advocate low-volatility strategies. Caveat: the portfolio construction and statistics were simple by later standards; subsequent studies confirmed the pattern with better methods but found it concentrated among the most volatile, often small and illiquid, stocks, and partly linked to exposures such as value, profitability and interest-rate sensitivity.

Ang, Hodrick, Xing and Zhang asked whether volatility, both market-wide and stock-specific, is priced in the cross-section of U.S. stock returns. First, they measured each stock's sensitivity to daily changes in market volatility, using changes in the VXO implied-volatility index as a proxy. Stocks whose returns rise when market volatility jumps act as insurance against bad times, and these stocks earned lower average returns, consistent with investors paying for protection against volatility risk. Second, and more surprisingly, stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility, measured as the standard deviation of the daily residuals e in r - r_f = a + b * MKT + s * SMB + h * HML + e over the past month, had very low subsequent average returns, so the most volatile group did markedly worse than the least volatile. This idiosyncratic volatility puzzle was not explained by size, book-to-market, momentum, liquidity, trading volume, coskewness or dispersion in analysts' forecasts. Rule: in their sample, high recent stock-specific volatility predicted low, not high, future returns. The paper became a cornerstone of the low-risk anomaly literature. Caveat: later work found the result sensitive to methodological choices such as portfolio weighting and how volatility is measured, explained part of it by short-term return reversal and by investors' taste for lottery-like stocks with extreme daily gains, and found that expected, rather than lagged, idiosyncratic volatility can relate positively to returns.

Baker, Bradley and Wurgler asked why the low-volatility anomaly, the long-standing tendency of low-risk stocks to earn returns as high as or higher than high-risk stocks, has persisted even though it is well known. Using U.S. stock data from the late 1960s to 2008, they confirmed that portfolios of low-volatility and low-beta stocks delivered both lower risk and higher returns than portfolios of high-volatility and high-beta stocks. They offered a two-part explanation. On the demand side, many investors are drawn to volatile stocks because of a preference for lottery-like payoffs, a tendency to treat exciting success stories as typical (representativeness) and overconfidence, which bids up their prices. On the supply side, the professionals who could correct the mispricing are judged against capitalisation-weighted benchmarks; for a manager judged by information ratio = (return - index return) / tracking error, buying low-beta stocks adds tracking error and tends to lag in rising markets, so the benchmark itself discourages exploiting the anomaly, a limit to arbitrage. Rule: a fixed benchmark mandate makes low-risk stocks look unattractive to managers even when they offer a better return per unit of absolute risk. Caveat: the evidence is historical and partly overlaps with value, profitability and interest-rate exposures, and the popularity of low-volatility funds after this paper may have reduced the premium by raising the valuations of low-risk stocks.

Frazzini and Pedersen asked why high-beta assets have earned less than the capital asset pricing model predicts, and proposed an answer based on borrowing limits. Many investors, such as individuals, pension funds and mutual funds, cannot or will not borrow. To reach a higher return target they overweight risky, high-beta assets instead of leveraging safe ones, which pushes up the prices of high-beta assets and lowers their future returns, flattening the relation between beta and return. Their model predicts the effect is stronger when funding is tight. To test it they built a betting-against-beta (BAB) factor: a portfolio that holds low-beta assets leveraged up to a beta of 1 and shorts high-beta assets scaled down to a beta of 1, so its overall market exposure is about zero. Rule: BAB return = (1 / beta_low) * (low-beta excess return) - (1 / beta_high) * (high-beta excess return). The factor earned significant risk-adjusted returns in U.S. equities, in many international stock markets, and in Treasury bonds, corporate bonds and futures, and its returns were lower when funding conditions worsened, as the theory predicts. Caveat: Novy-Marx and Velikov (2022) argued that much of BAB's performance comes from unusual construction choices, including rank weighting and beta shrinkage that overweight tiny stocks, and that implementable versions earn much less; others attribute the pattern to time-varying betas.

Rosenberg asked how to describe the way security returns move together more accurately than the single-index (market) model, which assumes that, once the market's influence is removed, stocks are unrelated. He showed that returns share substantial extra-market components of covariance: stocks in the same industry, or with similar characteristics, move together beyond what the market factor explains, so the single-index model misstates portfolio risk. He proposed representing these shared movements with a modest number of common factors tied to industries and company characteristics, which lets the full covariance matrix be estimated with far fewer free parameters than estimating every pair separately. Rule: return_i = the sum over factors k of (exposure of stock i to factor k) * (return of factor k) + specific return_i, so the covariance matrix = exposures * factor covariance * exposures transposed + a diagonal matrix of stock-specific variances. In related work he predicted exposures such as beta from fundamental company descriptors rather than from each stock's own price history. Rosenberg founded Barra, whose commercial multi-factor risk models built on this approach and became an industry standard for measuring portfolio risk. Caveat: the choice of factors and descriptors involves judgment, factor structures shift over time, and such models tend to underestimate risk in crises, when correlations rise suddenly and stock-specific risks start moving together.

Fama and MacBeth asked whether the capital asset pricing model's main predictions hold in NYSE data: that expected return rises linearly with beta, that nothing besides beta (such as beta squared or a stock's own residual risk) matters systematically, and that the reward for bearing beta risk is positive. Their method became a standard tool. Each month they ran a cross-sectional regression of returns on estimated betas and the other variables, producing a series of monthly slope estimates; they then averaged each slope over time and judged its significance with a t-statistic computed from the month-to-month variation of the estimates. Rule: t-statistic = average of the monthly slopes / (standard deviation of the monthly slopes / sqrt(number of months)). To reduce errors in the estimated betas they grouped stocks into portfolios ranked on betas estimated in an earlier period. Over 1935 to 1968 they found a positive average relation between beta and return, no systematic effect of beta squared or residual risk, and an intercept above the riskless rate, which fits Black's zero-beta version of the model better than the original. Caveat: the standard errors ignore the fact that betas are themselves estimated (Shanken's 1992 correction addresses this) and are biased when regression residuals are correlated over time, and data after 1963 showed a much flatter relation between beta and return.

Ross asked whether a theory of asset prices could be built without the strong assumptions of the capital asset pricing model, such as mean-variance preferences and an observable market portfolio. He assumed only that returns are generated by a linear factor model, return_i = expected return_i + the sum over k of b_ik * f_k + e_i, where the f_k are a few common factors with zero mean, the b_ik are each asset's sensitivities to them, and the e_i are asset-specific shocks that wash out in large, diversified portfolios. If investors could form a portfolio with no net cost and no factor exposure that still earned a positive expected return, that would be close to an arbitrage. Ruling out such opportunities forces expected returns to line up with factor sensitivities: expected return_i ~ lambda_0 + the sum over k of b_ik * lambda_k, where lambda_0 is the riskless (or zero-beta) rate and lambda_k is the risk premium per unit of exposure to factor k. The arbitrage pricing theory thus explains why only common, undiversifiable risks should carry a premium, without singling out the market portfolio. Caveat: the theory does not say what the factors are or how many there are, so empirical versions choose them by statistics or economic judgment, and the pricing relation is approximate and may fail for a few assets, which Shanken argued limits how well it can be tested.

Chen, Roll and Ross asked which economic forces are priced in the stock market, turning the arbitrage pricing theory's abstract factors into concrete macroeconomic ones. They argued that stock prices should respond to news that changes expected cash flows or discount rates, and constructed unexpected changes in several variables: industrial production growth, expected inflation, unanticipated inflation, the spread between low-grade and high-grade corporate bond yields (a gauge of the default risk premium), and the spread between long-term and short-term government bond yields (the term structure). Using the Fama-MacBeth two-step method, they estimated each stock portfolio's sensitivity to these surprises and tested whether those sensitivities explained average returns over 1958 to 1984. Industrial production, changes in the risk premium and twists in the yield curve were significantly priced, with weaker evidence for the inflation measures, while the stock market index, aggregate consumption and oil prices added no separate pricing power once the economic factors were included. Rule: expected return = risk-free rate + the sum over factors of (sensitivity to each macroeconomic surprise) * (premium for that surprise). Caveat: later re-examinations found the evidence fragile to the sample period and to how test portfolios and betas are formed, and macroeconomic factors explain only a small part of the month-to-month movement of individual stock returns.

Black and Scholes asked how to price an option on a stock using only quantities that can be observed, without knowing investors' attitudes to risk or the stock's expected return. They assumed the stock price follows a lognormal random walk with constant volatility, the interest rate is constant, there are no dividends, transaction costs or limits on borrowing and short selling, and trading is continuous. Under those conditions, a position combining the stock and the option in the right ratio is momentarily riskless, so it must earn the riskless rate, and that requirement pins down the option's price through a differential equation. The solution for a European call is C = S * N(d1) - K * exp(-r * T) * N(d2), with d1 = [ln(S / K) + (r + sigma^2 / 2) * T] / (sigma * sqrt(T)) and d2 = d1 - sigma * sqrt(T), where S is the stock price, K the strike, T the time to expiry, r the interest rate, sigma the volatility and N the standard normal cumulative distribution. The hedge ratio, delta = N(d1), says how many shares offset one option, the basis of delta hedging. The paper also noted that a company's shares can be viewed as a call option on the firm's assets, opening the way to pricing corporate debt. Caveat: real volatility is not constant, prices jump, and hedging is discrete and costly; since the 1987 crash, market prices imply different volatilities for different strikes (the smile), which the model cannot produce.

Merton asked which properties of option prices follow merely from the absence of dominance, meaning no security is held if another pays at least as much in every state and more in some, and then gave the Black-Scholes model a rigorous continuous-time foundation and several extensions. From dominance alone he derived bounds that any rational price must satisfy, for example that a call on a non-dividend-paying stock is worth at least max(0, S - K * exp(-r * T)), and showed that an American call on such a stock should never be exercised early, so it is worth the same as a European call. He clarified put-call parity, C - P = S - K * exp(-r * T) for European options, and explained why it does not hold exactly for American options, where early exercise of the put matters. Using Ito calculus, he re-derived the Black-Scholes formula under weaker conditions and extended it to stochastic interest rates, continuously paid dividends, and options whose payoff depends on the price path, such as down-and-out barrier options. The partial derivatives of his pricing formulas with respect to price, time, volatility and the interest rate are the sensitivities traders now call the Greeks. Caveat: the extensions keep the assumptions of continuous trading, no transaction costs and price paths without jumps; real markets violate these, and Merton himself added jumps in a 1976 paper.

Latané and Rendleman asked whether option prices reveal what the market expects a stock's future volatility to be. Since the Black-Scholes formula gives an option price for any assumed volatility, it can be run backwards: find the volatility that makes the formula's price equal the observed market price. They computed these implied standard deviations for options traded on the newly opened Chicago Board Options Exchange and combined the values from several options on the same stock into one weighted average, giving more weight to options whose prices are most sensitive to volatility. Rule: implied volatility = the sigma that solves Black-Scholes price(sigma) = market price, found numerically because no closed-form inverse exists. They found that these implied volatilities predicted subsequent realised volatility better than standard deviations computed from past returns, suggesting that option prices carry information beyond the historical record. This helped establish implied volatility as a market quantity in its own right, now quoted directly for many options and summarised in indexes such as the VIX. Caveat: different strikes and maturities on the same stock imply different volatilities (the smile), so any single implied figure depends on which options are averaged and how; implied volatility also contains a risk premium, and for index options it has typically exceeded the volatility later realised.

Stoll (1969), Journal of Finance 24(5), 801-824 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1969.tb01694.x | Topics: put-call parity

Stoll asked how the prices of puts and calls on the same stock should relate to each other in the over-the-counter options market of the 1960s, where dealers created one kind of option from the other through transactions known as conversions. He showed that a put can be manufactured from a call and the stock (and vice versa), together with borrowing or lending, so that, absent arbitrage, the call price minus the put price must equal the stock price minus the present value of the strike price. Rule (put-call parity, European form without dividends): C - P = S - K / (1 + r)^T. If the relationship were violated, a trader could buy the cheap side, sell the expensive side and lock in a riskless profit. He then examined prices quoted by put and call dealers and found that they broadly conformed to the relationship once the costs of financing and trading were taken into account. Parity means that a call price and the cost of carrying the stock are enough to determine the matching put price, and it underlies how traders build synthetic positions. Caveat: the exact equality holds only for options that can be exercised solely at expiry; Merton (1973) showed that with American options early exercise turns it into a pair of bounds, and in practice dividends, borrowing costs and short-sale constraints create persistent deviations.

Leland (1985), Journal of Finance 40(5), 1283-1301 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1985.tb02383.x | Topics: Black-Scholes; delta hedging; the Greeks

Leland asked how options can be priced and replicated when every trade costs money. In the Black-Scholes world the hedge is adjusted continuously, but with proportional transaction costs continuous trading would cost an unlimited amount, while infrequent rebalancing leaves hedging errors. Leland proposed rebalancing at fixed intervals of length dt and showed that the costs can be approximately absorbed by using an adjusted volatility in the Black-Scholes formula: adjusted sigma^2 = sigma^2 * (1 + sqrt(2 / pi) * k / (sigma * sqrt(dt))), where k is the round-trip proportional transaction cost. For someone replicating a long option position, which is how a writer hedges a short one, the volatility is raised, so the price including expected costs is above the frictionless Black-Scholes price, and the gap grows with the cost rate and with the rebalancing frequency. He argued that with this adjustment the hedging error tends to vanish as the rebalancing interval shrinks. The result gave practitioners a simple way to build transaction costs into option prices and into the portfolio-insurance strategies of the time. Caveat: later analysis (Kabanov and Safarian, 1997) showed that the hedging error does not fully vanish when the cost rate is held fixed as rebalancing becomes more frequent, the adjustment breaks down for payoffs that are not convex, and utility-based models with optimal rather than fixed-interval rebalancing perform better.

Hull (2018), Pearson; 10th edition (copyright 2018) | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://openlibrary.org/works/OL2691210W | Topics: Black-Scholes; implied volatility; put-call parity; delta hedging; the Greeks; binomial option pricing; volatility smile

Hull's textbook is the standard introduction to derivatives for students and practitioners, covering how futures, forwards, swaps and options work, how they are priced and how their risks are managed. It answers a practical question: given a derivative's contract terms and market data, what is it worth and how will its value respond as markets move? Topics include forward and futures pricing by cost of carry, interest rate and currency swaps, properties of stock options such as put-call parity, binomial trees, the Black-Scholes-Merton model, implied volatility and volatility smiles, numerical methods, exotic options, credit derivatives, value at risk and interest rate models. A central chapter defines the Greeks, the sensitivities used for hedging: delta = change in option value per unit change in the underlying price (N(d1) for a European call under Black-Scholes), gamma = rate of change of delta, vega = sensitivity to volatility, theta = sensitivity to the passage of time, and rho = sensitivity to the interest rate. The book shows how traders keep a portfolio delta-neutral by trading the underlying asset and use other options to control gamma and vega, and why hedges must be rebalanced as these sensitivities change. Caveat: it is a textbook that summarises market practice rather than original research, and the 10th edition predates the 2021-2023 retirement of LIBOR, so later editions should be consulted for interest-rate benchmarks and discounting conventions.

(1979), Journal of Financial Economics 7(3), 229-263 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(79)90015-1 | Topics: Black-Scholes; delta hedging; binomial option pricing

Cox, Ross and Rubinstein asked whether the economics of option pricing could be shown without the advanced mathematics of the Black-Scholes derivation. They modelled the stock price as moving, in each short period, either up by a factor u or down by a factor d. With one period left, a call can be replicated exactly by holding delta shares and borrowing, where delta = (C_up - C_down) / (S_up - S_down), so the option must cost the same as that replicating portfolio. The resulting price can be written as an expected payoff under special probabilities: option value = [p * C_up + (1 - p) * C_down] / R, with p = (R - d) / (u - d) and R = 1 + the riskless rate per period. Investors' actual beliefs about up and down moves drop out, which is the essence of risk-neutral valuation. Working backward through a tree of many periods prices options of any maturity, and checking at each node whether immediate exercise is worth more handles American options. Choosing u = exp(sigma * sqrt(dt)) and d = 1 / u makes the tree's answer converge to the Black-Scholes price as the number of steps grows. Caveat: convergence is slow and oscillates as the number of steps changes, so many steps or smoothing tricks are needed, and a constant-volatility tree cannot match the volatility smile seen in markets, which motivated implied trees.

Rubinstein asked how to build an option-pricing tree that agrees with the prices actually observed in the market, after noting that the Black-Scholes model, which had fitted S&P 500 index options reasonably well before the October 1987 crash, no longer did afterwards. Since the crash, index options with low strike prices have traded at much higher implied volatilities than those with high strikes, a pattern called the smile or skew, which means the market assigns more probability to large falls than a lognormal distribution does. Rubinstein's method first infers, from a set of option prices with the same expiration, the risk-neutral probabilities P_j of the index ending at each level j that stay closest to lognormal starting guesses Q_j, for example by minimising the sum of (P_j - Q_j)^2, while matching the observed prices. He then constructs a recombining binomial tree consistent with that distribution, assuming that all paths leading to the same final node are equally likely. Rule: the market's option prices fix the probabilities at the end of the tree, and working backward fills in the rest, so American and exotic options can be priced consistently with the observed smile. Caveat: the method fits a single expiration and relies on a strong assumption about path probabilities; Derman and Kani and Dupire generalised it to many maturities, and models of this local-volatility type predict smile movements that are inconsistent with how markets actually behave, which hurts their hedges.

QUANT LIBRARY | SUMMARY in our own words (not the work's text) | "Pricing with a Smile" by Bruno Dupire (1994), Risk 7(1), 18-20 (January 1994) | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://www.risk.net/derivatives/equity-derivatives/1500211/pricing-with-a-smile | Topics: implied volatility; volatility smile

Dupire asked whether the volatility smile, the fact that options on the same asset with different strikes and maturities imply different volatilities, can be reproduced by a model in which the asset price still follows a single-factor diffusion. He showed that it can, and that the answer is unique: if European call prices are known for all strikes K and maturities T, there is exactly one local volatility function sigma(S, t), depending on the asset price and time, consistent with all of them. With no dividends and a constant interest rate r, the formula is sigma_local^2(K, T) = [dC/dT + r * K * dC/dK] / [0.5 * K^2 * d2C/dK2], where C(K, T) is the surface of call prices and the derivatives are partial derivatives. The denominator is tied to the risk-neutral probability density of the asset at T, which Breeden and Litzenberger had shown can be read from the curvature of call prices across strikes. Once calibrated, the local volatility model prices exotic options consistently with the market for standard options. Dupire's continuous-time result appeared in the same year as Derman and Kani's tree-based version. Caveat: the formula requires a smooth, arbitrage-free interpolation of market quotes and is numerically unstable for far-out strikes; local volatility also predicts that the smile shifts the opposite way to what is observed when the asset price moves (Hagan and co-authors, 2002), which led to stochastic volatility models such as SABR for hedging.

Engle (1982), Econometrica 50(4), 987-1007 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.2307/1912773 | Topics: volatility; GARCH

Engle asked how to model a time series whose uncertainty changes over time, so that forecasts come with error bands that widen in turbulent periods and narrow in calm ones. Standard models assumed that the variance of shocks was constant. He proposed autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH), in which today's variance depends on the size of recent shocks: h_t = alpha_0 + alpha_1 * e_(t-1)^2 + ... + alpha_q * e_(t-q)^2, where e is the unexpected part of the series and h_t is the variance expected for period t given the past. A large surprise yesterday raises the variance expected today, so big moves cluster together while their direction stays unpredictable. He showed how to estimate the model by maximum likelihood and provided a simple test for ARCH effects: regress squared residuals on their own lags and compare the sample size times the R-squared with a chi-squared distribution. Applied to inflation in the United Kingdom, the model showed that inflation uncertainty varied substantially over time. It was soon applied to financial returns, where volatility clustering is pronounced, and Engle shared the 2003 Nobel prize in economics for this work. Caveat: capturing the slow decay of volatility needs many lags, which GARCH addressed; ARCH treats good and bad news symmetrically; and with normally distributed shocks it still underestimates the fat tails of returns.

QUANT LIBRARY | SUMMARY in our own words (not the work's text) | "Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity" by Tim Bollerslev (1986), Journal of Econometrics 31(3), 307-327 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4076(86)90063-1 | Topics: volatility; GARCH

Bollerslev asked how to make Engle's ARCH model more economical. Pure ARCH models often needed many lagged squared shocks to describe how slowly volatility fades, with many parameters to estimate and constrain. Bollerslev's generalized ARCH (GARCH) adds lags of the conditional variance itself, so a short formula captures long memory in volatility. The workhorse GARCH(1,1) is h_t = omega + alpha * e_(t-1)^2 + beta * h_(t-1): today's variance is a constant plus a fraction of yesterday's squared surprise plus a fraction of yesterday's variance. The process is stationary if alpha + beta < 1, its long-run average variance is omega / (1 - alpha - beta), and alpha + beta measures how persistent volatility shocks are. He set out the conditions for the model to be well behaved, showed how to estimate it by maximum likelihood, and applied it to U.S. inflation. GARCH(1,1) became the default volatility model in finance, and the exponentially weighted moving average used by RiskMetrics is the special case with omega = 0 and alpha + beta = 1. Caveat: fitted values of alpha + beta are often very close to 1, which may reflect structural breaks rather than true persistence; the model responds equally to good and bad news, which GJR and EGARCH variants correct; and normally distributed shocks understate tail risk, which is why Student-t versions are common.

(1993), Journal of Finance 48(5), 1779-1801 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1993.tb05128.x | Topics: GARCH; GJR-GARCH

Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle asked how the expected excess return on U.S. stocks relates to their volatility, a question on which earlier studies disagreed. They argued that the standard GARCH-in-mean model was too restrictive and modified it in several ways: allowing seasonal patterns, letting the nominal interest rate help predict volatility, and, most influentially, letting positive and negative surprises affect future volatility differently. Their asymmetric volatility equation is h_t = omega + alpha * e_(t-1)^2 + gamma * I_(t-1) * e_(t-1)^2 + beta * h_(t-1), where I_(t-1) equals 1 if the previous surprise was negative and 0 otherwise, so a bad-news shock raises volatility by (alpha + gamma) times its square while a good-news shock raises it by alpha times its square. In monthly U.S. data they found that negative surprises raised volatility while positive surprises tended to lower it, that volatility was less persistent than standard models suggested, and, with these modifications, that the conditional expected excess return was negatively related to conditional volatility, contrary to the simple notion that higher risk always brings a higher expected return. The asymmetric equation is now known as GJR-GARCH. Caveat: the estimated sign of the risk-return relation depends heavily on the model specification and conditioning information, and other studies using different methods have found a positive relation, so the question remains unsettled.

Moreira and Muir asked whether investors can improve returns by taking less risk when volatility is high and more when it is low. If expected returns rose in proportion to volatility, cutting exposure in turbulent times would sacrifice return; they found instead that, in the short run, volatility rises much more than expected returns do. Their strategy scales a factor's return each month by the inverse of its realised variance over the previous month: managed return(t+1) = (c / previous month's variance) * factor return(t+1), with the constant c chosen so that the managed and original portfolios have the same overall volatility. Applied to the stock market and to factors such as value, momentum, profitability, return on equity, investment, betting against beta and the currency carry trade, the volatility-managed versions produced positive alphas relative to the unmanaged factors and raised the market's Sharpe ratio, with especially large gains for momentum. They argued that this is hard to reconcile with standard asset-pricing models in which risk premiums rise sharply in bad times. Rule: reduce exposure when recent volatility is high and increase it when volatility is low. Caveat: Cederburg and co-authors (2020) found that the improvements largely disappear for most factors in realistic out-of-sample implementations, and trading costs and leverage limits reduce the gains further.

(2018), Journal of Portfolio Management 45(1), 14-33 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2018.45.1.014 | Topics: volatility; fat tails; volatility targeting

Harvey, Hoyle, Korgaonkar, Rattray, Sargaison and Van Hemert, mostly practitioners at the asset manager Man Group, asked what volatility targeting actually does for different assets: does scaling a position to keep its volatility near a constant target improve risk-adjusted returns, and does it reduce extreme outcomes? Using long histories of equities, government bonds, credit, currencies and commodities, they compared buy-and-hold positions with versions rescaled each period by target volatility divided by a recent volatility estimate. Rule: position size = target volatility / forecast volatility, so exposure falls when markets turn turbulent. For risk assets such as equities and credit, targeting raised Sharpe ratios, which they linked to the leverage effect: volatility tends to rise when prices fall, so cutting exposure as volatility rises avoids part of the losses. For bonds, currencies and commodities the effect on Sharpe ratios was small. Across all asset classes, however, volatility targeting reduced the likelihood of extreme returns, trimming the left tail and making realised volatility more stable over time. Caveat: the method reacts to volatility only after it has risen, so it cannot shield a position from a sudden gap or a crash that arrives out of a calm market; frequent rebalancing costs money; and the results depend on the choice of volatility estimator and target.

Qian asked whether the traditional balanced portfolio, about 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds, is as diversified as it looks. Measuring each asset's contribution to total portfolio risk rather than its share of capital, he showed that because stocks are far more volatile than bonds, over 90 percent of such a portfolio's risk comes from stocks, so its returns are dominated by the stock market. He coined the term risk parity for portfolios in which each asset class contributes equally to total risk. Rule: the risk contribution of asset i = w_i * (covariance of asset i with the portfolio) / portfolio volatility; these contributions add up to the portfolio's volatility, and a risk-parity portfolio sets them equal. With two assets this means weights exactly in inverse proportion to their volatilities, so bonds receive far more capital than in a 60/40 mix, and the approach extends to other asset classes such as commodities. Because an unlevered risk-parity portfolio has low risk and low return, leverage is applied to bring it to the desired risk level, and Qian argued that the result can deliver a higher return per unit of risk than the traditional mix. Caveat: the paper comes from an asset manager that offers risk-parity funds; the strategy's historical success depended on leveraged bonds during a long period of falling interest rates, and in 2022, when stocks and bonds fell together as rates rose, risk-parity funds suffered large losses.

(2010), Journal of Portfolio Management 36(4), 60-70 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2010.36.4.060 | Topics: diversification; risk parity

Maillard, Roncalli and Teïletche asked what mathematical properties the equally weighted risk contribution (ERC) portfolio has, the portfolio in which every asset contributes the same amount to total risk. With weights w and covariance matrix Sigma, portfolio volatility sigma(w) splits exactly into contributions w_i * (Sigma * w)_i / sigma(w), and the ERC portfolio sets all of these equal. They proved that for a long-only portfolio such a portfolio exists and is unique, and that its volatility lies between those of two familiar portfolios: sigma(minimum variance) <= sigma(ERC) <= sigma(equal weights). ERC is therefore a middle ground between minimising risk, which tends to concentrate in a few low-volatility assets, and naive equal weighting, which ignores risk altogether. When all pairwise correlations are equal, ERC weights are simply proportional to 1 / volatility. They also showed that ERC is the minimum-variance portfolio subject to the sum of the logarithms of the weights staying above a threshold, a constraint that keeps the weights spread out, and gave numerical algorithms and examples for the general case. Caveat: ERC ignores expected returns and is optimal in the Sharpe-ratio sense only under special conditions, such as equal Sharpe ratios and constant correlations; results depend on covariance estimates and on how the investable universe is divided into assets, since splitting one asset class into several changes its share of the risk budget.

(2012), Financial Analysts Journal 68(1), 47-59 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.2469/faj.v68.n1.1 | Topics: CAPM; low-volatility anomaly; risk parity

Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen asked why risk parity portfolios, which balance risk across asset classes and then apply leverage, have historically outperformed traditional portfolios such as 60 percent stocks and 40 percent bonds, and whether there is an economic reason to expect this. Their argument is leverage aversion: many investors cannot or will not borrow, so when they want higher expected returns they tilt toward riskier assets such as stocks instead of leveraging safer ones. That demand pushes up the prices of risky assets and lowers their risk-adjusted returns, making the relation between risk and return flatter than standard theory predicts. A risk parity investor willing to use leverage holds more of the safer, relatively under-priced assets and so can earn a higher return per unit of risk. Rule: levered return = L * (portfolio return - risk-free rate) + risk-free rate, so leverage scales excess return and risk together and keeps the Sharpe ratio; if the risk-return line is too flat, the better portfolio is a higher-Sharpe-ratio, lower-risk mix scaled up with leverage. Using U.S. data from 1926 to 2010, they found that a risk parity portfolio of stocks and bonds had a higher Sharpe ratio than both the market portfolio and the 60/40 portfolio, with similar results in global data. Caveat: the long backtest includes decades of falling interest rates that favoured leveraged bonds; leverage brings financing costs and margin risk; and Anderson, Bianchi and Goldberg (2012) found that realistic trading and financing costs erode much of the advantage.

Black and Litterman asked why mean-variance optimisation so rarely produced sensible portfolios in practice, and how to fix it. When investors plug in their own estimates of expected returns, optimisers recommend extreme, unstable positions that swing wildly with small changes in inputs, because the inputs are noisy. Their solution starts from a neutral reference point: the expected returns that would make the global market-capitalisation portfolio optimal, found by reverse optimisation, implied returns = risk-aversion coefficient * covariance matrix * market weights. The investor then states views, absolute or relative (for example, that one country's bonds will beat another's by a stated margin), each with a confidence level. The model blends the equilibrium returns with the views, weighting each by its precision, in the manner of Bayesian updating: blended returns = [(tau * Sigma)^-1 + P' * Omega^-1 * P]^-1 * [(tau * Sigma)^-1 * Pi + P' * Omega^-1 * Q], where Pi holds the equilibrium returns, P and Q describe the views, Omega their uncertainty and tau scales the uncertainty of the equilibrium estimate. The optimiser then produces portfolios that depart from market weights only in the direction of the views, by amounts that reflect confidence. They illustrated the approach with a global portfolio of bonds, equities and currencies. Caveat: tau and Omega are hard to choose and change results materially, and the starting point assumes that the market portfolio is efficient, as in the capital asset pricing model.

He and Litterman asked why the Black-Litterman model behaves as it does, aiming to give portfolio managers intuition rather than new theory. They showed that, without constraints, the model's optimal portfolio has a simple structure: it equals the market-capitalisation portfolio, scaled down slightly to reflect uncertainty about the equilibrium returns, plus a weighted sum of portfolios that each represent one of the investor's views. Rule: optimal weights = (market weights + P' * Lambda) / (1 + tau), where each column of P' is the portfolio expressing one view and Lambda contains the weights placed on those view portfolios. A view receives more weight when it departs further from what equilibrium already implies, when the investor's confidence in it is higher, and when it is less correlated with the other views; a view that agrees with equilibrium changes nothing, and with no views the investor simply holds the market. They walked through worked examples with several national equity markets to show how changing the strength of, or confidence in, a view tilts the portfolio. This made it easy to check that a model portfolio actually reflects the manager's intentions. Caveat: the clean result assumes no constraints and a known covariance matrix; the meaning and choice of tau and of view confidences remain debated, and later work, such as Idzorek's, proposed more intuitive ways to specify confidence.

QUANT LIBRARY | SUMMARY in our own words (not the work's text) | "Co-Integration and Error Correction: Representation, Estimation, and Testing" by Robert F. Engle and Clive W. J. Granger (1987), Econometrica 55(2), 251-276 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.2307/1913236 | Topics: hypothesis testing; mean reversion; statistical arbitrage

Engle and Granger asked how to model economic series that wander like random walks individually but appear tied together over the long run, such as consumption and income, or short and long interest rates. They defined cointegration: two non-stationary series are cointegrated if some linear combination of them is stationary, so their spread keeps returning to a stable relationship even though each series drifts. The Granger representation theorem shows that cointegrated series can be written in error-correction form: each period, part of the previous deviation from the long-run relationship is corrected, so the size of the deviation helps predict future changes. They proposed a two-step procedure: estimate the long-run relation by ordinary least squares, y_t = a + b * x_t + u_t, then test whether the residual u_t is stationary with a Dickey-Fuller-type test using special critical values, and, if it is, use the lagged residual in an error-correction model of the changes. Rule: spread_t = y_t - b * x_t is mean-reverting when y and x are cointegrated, even though y and x are not. This framework is the formal basis for pairs and spread trading. Engle and Granger shared the 2003 Nobel prize in economics. Caveat: the two-step test has low power, results can depend on which variable is placed on the left, it finds at most one relationship (Johansen's method handles several), and cointegration between securities can break when the economics behind it changes.

(2006), Review of Financial Studies 19(3), 797-827 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hhj020 | Topics: backtesting; mean reversion; statistical arbitrage

Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst asked whether pairs trading, a strategy long used on Wall Street trading desks, actually makes money, and what explains its returns. Their rule is simple and avoids fitting a model. In a 12-month formation period, each stock's price series is normalised to a cumulative total-return index and paired with the stock whose index stays closest to it, measured by the sum of squared differences. In the following six-month trading period, when a pair's spread, the gap between their normalised prices, exceeds 2 * its historical standard deviation, the strategy buys the loser and sells the winner, closing the position when the prices cross again or the period ends. Applied to U.S. stocks from 1962 to 2002, the best pairs portfolios earned annualised excess returns of up to about 11 percent, comfortably above conservative estimates of transaction costs, and the profits were not explained by simple short-term reversal. They interpreted the profits as a reward to arbitrageurs for enforcing the law of one price between close substitutes. Rule: trade the spread between two historically similar stocks when it is unusually wide, betting that it will close. Caveat: profits declined in the later years of the sample, and studies of more recent data found that after realistic trading costs the returns are modest; the distance rule has no model of why a spread should close, so pairs can drift apart permanently.

Avellaneda and Lee asked how a model-driven statistical arbitrage strategy in U.S. equities can be built and how such strategies performed. Each stock's daily return is split into a part explained by common factors and an idiosyncratic residual. The factors come either from principal component analysis of the stock correlation matrix (eigenportfolios) or from sector exchange-traded funds. The cumulative residual of each stock is modelled as a mean-reverting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, and each stock gets an s-score: how many equilibrium standard deviations its residual sits from its estimated mean. Rule: s = (X(t) - m) / sigma_eq; sell the stock and hedge with the factors when s is well above zero, buy when it is well below, close the trade when s returns near zero, and trade only stocks whose residuals revert quickly enough. Backtests from the late 1990s to 2007 showed attractive Sharpe ratios for the principal-component version, somewhat lower ones for the sector-ETF version, and weaker performance after the early 2000s; measuring signals in trading time, using volume information, improved results. They also analysed August 2007, when many quantitative equity funds lost money at once as similar positions were unwound. Caveat: the backtests assume modest transaction costs and involve design choices made with hindsight, and crowding by funds running similar strategies leaves such portfolios exposed to sudden simultaneous deleveraging, as August 2007 showed.

Bailey and Marcos López de Prado (2014), Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5), 94-107 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2014.40.5.094 | Topics: Sharpe ratio; backtesting; hypothesis testing; backtest overfitting

Bailey and López de Prado asked how to judge a backtested Sharpe ratio when it was selected as the best of many attempts. Trying many strategy variations raises the highest Sharpe ratio found even if none has real skill, and short samples, skewed returns and fat tails make the estimate less reliable still. Their deflated Sharpe ratio corrects for both problems. First, estimate the Sharpe ratio one would expect from the best of N independent trials with no skill: expected maximum SR ~ sqrt(variance of the trials' Sharpe ratios) * [(1 - gamma) * Z^-1(1 - 1/N) + gamma * Z^-1(1 - 1/(N * e))], where gamma ~ 0.5772 is the Euler-Mascheroni constant and Z^-1 is the inverse of the standard normal distribution. Second, compute the probability that the observed ratio beats that hurdle, adjusting for the sample length T, skewness and kurtosis: DSR = Z[(SR - SR_0) * sqrt(T - 1) / sqrt(1 - skewness * SR + (kurtosis - 1) / 4 * SR^2)], where SR_0 is the expected maximum and Z the standard normal distribution. A DSR close to 1, such as above 0.95, suggests the result is unlikely to be a statistical fluke. They argued that researchers should record and report the number of trials behind every backtest. Caveat: the method needs the number of effectively independent trials and the variance of their Sharpe ratios, which are rarely recorded and hard to estimate when trials are correlated, and it relies on large-sample approximations.

Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu, writing for mathematicians, asked how easy it is to produce an impressive-looking investment backtest by accident. They showed that if a researcher tries enough variations of a strategy on the same historical data, a high in-sample Sharpe ratio is almost guaranteed even when every variation has zero true skill. They derived the minimum backtest length (MinBTL): the number of years of data needed so that the best of N independent zero-skill configurations is not expected to reach a given annualised Sharpe ratio. Approximately, MinBTL < 2 * ln(N) / (E[max Sharpe])^2, so the data required grows with the logarithm of the number of trials; for example, with five years of data, trying more than about 45 independent configurations makes an annualised Sharpe ratio of 1 expected from luck alone. They also argued that when returns have memory, such as mean reversion, overfit strategies tend to do worse than zero out of sample, because the chosen parameters chase patterns that then reverse. They called on journals and investment firms to require disclosure of the number of trials behind any backtest. Caveat: the formulas assume independent trials and normally distributed returns, so with correlated trials the effective number is smaller than the raw count; the bound says how likely a fluke is but not whether a particular strategy is overfit, which their later probability-of-backtest-overfitting method addressed.

Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu asked how to estimate the probability that the strategy configuration chosen as best in a backtest is overfit, meaning that its in-sample rank owes more to noise than to skill. They argued that the usual hold-out approach, testing on one reserved slice of data, is unreliable for backtests because that slice is arbitrary and small. Their method, combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV), starts from a matrix of returns for all N configurations tried over T periods. The rows are split into S equal blocks; for every way of choosing half the blocks as the in-sample set, with the rest as the out-of-sample set, they find the configuration with the best in-sample performance and record its relative rank out of sample. Rule: PBO = the fraction of these splits in which the in-sample winner ranks below the median out of sample (equivalently, the logit of its relative rank falls below zero). A PBO near 0 means the selection process tends to pick genuinely better configurations; near 0.5 or above, the selection is no better than chance. The same calculations show how much performance typically degrades from in-sample to out-of-sample and how often the chosen strategy loses money. Caveat: the method needs a full record of every configuration tried and assumes performance is comparable across blocks of time, so serial dependence and regime changes can distort the estimate, and a low PBO alone does not mean the chosen strategy will be profitable.

Harvey, Liu and Zhu asked how many of the hundreds of factors claimed to explain the cross-section of stock returns are likely to be real. They catalogued 316 factors proposed in published research and working papers, with the pace of new proposals accelerating in recent decades, and argued that with so much testing on the same data the usual standard of statistical significance, a t-statistic above about 2, is far too lenient: some factors will clear it by luck alone. Using multiple-testing frameworks from statistics that control either the family-wise error rate (Bonferroni, Holm) or the false discovery rate (Benjamini, Hochberg and Yekutieli), and allowing for tests that were run but never published, they estimated how the significance hurdle should rise over time as more factors are tried. Rule: with M tests, the Bonferroni method requires each p-value < 0.05 / M; in their calibration, a newly proposed factor should clear a t-statistic of about 3.0 rather than 2.0, and the threshold should keep rising as research continues. Under these standards a large share of published factors would be judged likely false discoveries, and the authors suggested that many claimed findings in financial economics are probably false. Caveat: the adjusted thresholds depend on assumptions about the unobserved number of tests and their correlation, and later work, such as Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen (2023), argued with Bayesian methods that most factors replicate reasonably well once their economic similarity is taken into account.

Demsetz asked what it costs to trade a stock and what determines that cost. Beyond brokerage commissions, a trader who wants to buy or sell right away must accept the price offered by someone standing ready to trade, paying a little above or receiving a little below the prevailing value. He argued that the bid-ask spread is the price of this immediacy: dealers and specialists stand ready to trade at any time, and the spread is how they are paid for providing that service. Rule: spread = ask - bid, and the cost of an immediate round trip, buying and then selling, is about one spread, so one side costs roughly spread / 2. Using New York Stock Exchange data, he found that spreads were narrower for stocks with more trading activity, consistent with economies of scale, since frequent trading lowers the cost and the waiting time of matching buyers with sellers, and he stressed that competition from other traders' orders limits how wide spreads can become. The paper launched the economic study of how trading mechanisms set transaction costs, now called market microstructure. Caveat: Demsetz focused on the cost of supplying immediacy and processing orders; later theories showed that the spread also compensates dealers for inventory risk (Ho and Stoll) and for losses to better-informed traders (Glosten and Milgrom), components his framework did not model, and modern electronic markets have very different cost structures.
