Roll asked whether the effective bid-ask spread, the trading cost actually paid, can be inferred from a series of transaction prices alone, without quote data. In an efficient market where the underlying value follows a random walk, trades fall unpredictably at the bid or at the ask, so recorded prices bounce up and down by the spread. That bounce creates negative correlation between successive price changes: a trade at the ask tends to be followed by a lower recorded price, and a trade at the bid by a higher one. If buys and sells are equally likely and the spread s is constant, the covariance of successive price changes equals -s^2 / 4. Rule: estimated spread = 2 * sqrt(-covariance of consecutive price changes). He applied the measure to daily and weekly returns of U.S. stocks and found that the implied spreads were related to firm size as expected, with smaller firms showing larger spreads. Its appeal is that it needs nothing but prices, so it can be used where quotes are unavailable, such as in long historical data. Caveat: when the sample covariance is positive, which happens often, especially with daily data, the formula has no real solution; the estimate is noisy and is biased when new information arrives with trades, when quotes adjust to inventory, or when order flow is persistent. Later estimators, such as Hasbrouck's Bayesian version and the Corwin-Schultz high-low method, address some of these problems.

Corwin and Paul Schultz (2012), Journal of Finance 67(2), 719-760 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2012.01729.x | Topics: volatility; order book spread

Corwin and Schultz asked how to estimate the bid-ask spread from daily high and low prices, which exist for long histories and many markets where quote data do not. Their insight is that the daily high is usually a trade at the ask and the daily low a trade at the bid, so the ratio of high to low reflects both the stock's volatility and its spread. The two components behave differently over time: the volatility part of the squared log range grows in proportion to the length of the interval, while the spread part does not. Comparing the price range over single days with the range over two consecutive days therefore lets the two be separated. Rule: with beta = the sum over the two days of [ln(High / Low)]^2 and gamma = [ln(two-day High / two-day Low)]^2, set alpha = (sqrt(2 * beta) - sqrt(beta)) / (3 - 2 * sqrt(2)) - sqrt(gamma / (3 - 2 * sqrt(2))); the spread is then S = 2 * (exp(alpha) - 1) / (1 + exp(alpha)). Compared with spreads measured from intraday trade and quote data, their estimator was more accurate in their tests than other low-frequency measures, including Roll's. Caveat: it can produce negative estimates, which are usually set to zero; overnight price moves must be adjusted for; and it is least reliable for very liquid stocks, where the spread is tiny relative to volatility, and in markets with infrequent trading.

Amihud asked whether a simple measure of illiquidity, computable from daily data available over long periods, explains differences in stock returns across stocks and over time. His measure, ILLIQ, is the average over days of the absolute return divided by the dollar trading volume: ILLIQ = average of |daily return| / daily dollar volume. It captures how much the price moves per dollar traded, a rough gauge of price impact in the spirit of Kyle's lambda. Using NYSE stocks from the 1960s to the late 1990s, he found that across stocks, more illiquid stocks earned higher average returns, consistent with investors demanding compensation for trading costs. Over time, higher expected market illiquidity went with higher expected excess returns, while unexpected increases in illiquidity lowered stock prices at the time, and these effects were stronger for small stocks. Rule: illiquidity is priced; investors require a premium to hold assets that are costly to trade, and a rise in market-wide illiquidity hurts prices, especially those of small, illiquid stocks. The measure became one of the most widely used liquidity proxies because it needs only returns and volume. Caveat: ILLIQ mixes volatility with liquidity and is strongly related to firm size; its level drifts with inflation and with the growth of trading volume, so it must be rescaled over time; and comparisons with high-frequency benchmarks find that it captures price impact better than it captures spreads.

Stoll (1981), Journal of Financial Economics 9(1), 47-73 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(81)90020-9 | Topics: market maker; market-maker inventory risk; market makers set the spread

Ho and Stoll asked how a dealer who stands ready to buy and sell a stock should set the prices at which it buys (the bid) and sells (the ask). The dealer faces two kinds of uncertainty: buy and sell orders arrive randomly, at rates that depend on how attractive the quotes are, and any inventory the dealer accumulates can lose value because the stock's return is uncertain. Solving for the quotes that maximise the dealer's expected utility of wealth over a trading horizon, they found that the spread compensates for the risk of holding inventory: it widens with the dealer's risk aversion, the variance of the stock's return and the size of transactions, depends on the time remaining in the horizon, and reflects how strongly order arrivals respond to the quotes. Inventory affects where the quotes sit rather than how wide they are: a dealer who has accumulated too much stock lowers both bid and ask to attract buyers and discourage further sellers, and raises both when short. Rule: bid = reservation price - half-spread and ask = reservation price + half-spread, where the reservation price shifts against the inventory held and the half-spread reflects risk and order-flow conditions. This model of inventory risk is a direct ancestor of modern market-making algorithms such as Avellaneda and Stoikov's. Caveat: it assumes a single monopolistic dealer and no informed traders; empirical studies find that inventory costs explain only part of observed spreads, with adverse selection and order-processing costs accounting for the rest.

Avellaneda and Stoikov asked how a market maker in an electronic limit order book should place its buy and sell quotes to earn the spread while controlling the risk of the inventory it accumulates. They assumed the mid-price follows a random walk with volatility sigma, that the market maker's orders are filled at rates that fall exponentially with their distance from the mid-price, lambda(delta) = A * exp(-k * delta), and that the market maker maximises the expected exponential utility, with risk aversion gamma, of wealth at a horizon T. The solution has two parts. First, a reservation price, the market maker's own valuation adjusted for inventory: r = s - q * gamma * sigma^2 * (T - t), where s is the mid-price and q the inventory, so a market maker who is long values the stock below the mid. Second, a total spread around that reservation price: delta_ask + delta_bid = gamma * sigma^2 * (T - t) + (2 / gamma) * ln(1 + gamma / k). Quotes are placed symmetrically around r, so inventory skews them, encouraging trades that bring inventory back toward zero. Simulations showed that this inventory-aware quoting gave lower profit variance than quoting symmetrically around the mid-price. Caveat: the model assumes constant volatility and fill rates, no adverse selection from informed traders and no limit on inventory, and its dependence on a fixed end time is unnatural for continuous trading; Guéant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia later solved a bounded-inventory version with stable quotes.

(2013), Mathematics and Financial Economics 7(4), 477-507 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11579-012-0087-0 | Topics: market maker; market-maker inventory risk

Guéant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia asked how to solve exactly the market maker's quoting problem posed by Avellaneda and Stoikov when inventory must stay within limits. They kept the same ingredients (a Brownian mid-price with volatility sigma, fill rates A * exp(-k * delta) falling with a quote's distance delta from the mid, and risk aversion gamma) and added a maximum position size. After a change of variables, the nonlinear equations for the optimal quotes reduce to a system of linear ordinary differential equations with a closed-form solution involving a matrix exponential. Far from the end of the horizon the quotes settle to stationary values that depend only on inventory, removing the arbitrary time dependence of the earlier model. Their closed-form approximation: each quote sits a base distance (1 / gamma) * ln(1 + gamma / k) from the mid, plus or minus an inventory adjustment in units of u = sqrt(sigma^2 * gamma / (2 * k * A) * (1 + gamma / k)^(1 + k / gamma)); the total spread is about twice the base distance plus one u, and the midpoint of the quotes shifts against an inventory of q by about q * u. At the position limit the market maker stops quoting on the side that would breach it. Caveat: the model still assumes Brownian prices, exponential fill rates, constant parameters and no adverse selection; real use needs careful calibration of A and k, and it leaves out fees, tick sizes and queue position, which matter in practice.

Milgrom (1985), Journal of Financial Economics 14(1), 71-100 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(85)90044-3 | Topics: order book spread; market maker; informed traders vs market makers; market makers set the spread

Glosten and Milgrom asked why a bid-ask spread would exist even if dealers had no costs and bore no inventory risk. In their model a competitive, risk-neutral specialist trades one unit at a time with a sequence of traders, some of whom know the asset's true value while others trade for reasons unrelated to information. Because the specialist cannot tell who is informed, every buy order is partly bad news: it is more likely to come from someone who knows the value is high. The specialist therefore sets the ask equal to the expected value of the asset given that a buy order has arrived, and the bid equal to its expected value given that a sell order has arrived. Rule: ask = E[value | buy order], bid = E[value | sell order], so the spread is a pure adverse-selection cost, wider when more traders are informed or when their private information matters more. What the specialist loses to informed traders is recovered from uninformed ones. Transaction prices follow a martingale, and as trading reveals information they converge toward the true value. If informed trading is too prevalent, the spread can become so wide that trade stops altogether. Caveat: the model allows only single-unit trades and ignores inventory and processing costs; empirical decompositions find adverse selection is one important component of spreads alongside others, and modern electronic market makers face it in the form of fast, well-informed order flow.

Kyle (1985), Econometrica 53(6), 1315-1335 | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.2307/1913210 | Topics: informed traders vs market makers; market impact

Kyle asked how an insider with private information about an asset's value should trade, and how prices come to reflect that information. In his model a single risk-neutral insider knows the asset's value, noise traders submit random orders, and competitive market makers see only the combined order flow and set the price equal to the asset's expected value given that flow. The insider trades strategically, hiding orders among the noise traders. In the single-auction equilibrium, the insider's order is proportional to the gap between the true value and the prior price, and the price moves linearly with net order flow: price change = lambda * (insider order + noise orders), with lambda = (standard deviation of value) / (2 * standard deviation of noise trading). Half of the insider's information ends up in the price. Lambda measures price impact, and its inverse, market depth, is the order flow needed to move the price by one unit; markets are deeper when there is more noise trading. In the continuous-trading version the insider trades gradually, so that information enters the price at a steady rate and is fully reflected by the end, while depth stays constant over time. Rule: price impact is linear in signed order flow, scaled by how much private information exists relative to noise trading. Caveat: the linear impact relies on normal distributions and a single risk-neutral insider; empirical studies of large orders find impact rising roughly with the square root of size, and real markets have many competing informed traders.

Almgren and Chriss asked how to break a large order into smaller trades over a fixed period so as to balance two opposing costs: trading quickly moves the price against you (market impact), while trading slowly leaves the unexecuted position exposed to random price moves. They modelled the price as a random walk with volatility sigma and two kinds of impact: permanent impact, which shifts the price for the rest of the period in proportion to the amount traded, and temporary impact, which affects only the current trade in proportion to the trading rate. For a trader who minimises expected cost plus lambda times the variance of cost, the optimal schedule has a closed form: holdings at time t = X * sinh(kappa * (T - t)) / sinh(kappa * T), where X is the initial position, T the deadline and kappa ~ sqrt(lambda * sigma^2 / eta), with eta the temporary-impact coefficient. A risk-neutral trader (lambda = 0) trades at a constant rate, the familiar time-weighted schedule, while a more risk-averse trader sells faster at the start. Varying lambda traces an efficient frontier of trading strategies in expected cost and variance, analogous to Markowitz's frontier for portfolios. The model became the standard starting point for execution algorithms. Caveat: impact is assumed linear and constant, whereas empirical studies of large orders find concave impact, roughly growing with the square root of size, that partly decays after trading stops; later models add this transient impact and order-book dynamics.

Almgren, Thum, Hauptmann and Li asked how the market impact of large stock orders depends on order size, trading speed and the stock's characteristics, using a large data set of actual institutional orders executed by Citigroup's U.S. equity trading desks. Building on the Almgren-Chriss framework, they separated permanent impact, the lasting price shift that remains after an order is complete, from temporary impact, the extra cost paid while trading, and estimated how each scales. They found permanent impact roughly linear in order size measured as a fraction of daily volume, scaled by the stock's volatility and adjusted for how often its shares turn over, and temporary impact growing with the trading rate raised to a power of about 3/5. Rule: temporary cost per share ~ eta * sigma * (shares traded per unit time / daily volume)^(3/5), where sigma is daily volatility, so trading twice as fast raises the cost per share by roughly 50 percent rather than doubling it. The results were designed to feed directly into optimal trade-scheduling algorithms and into pre-trade and post-trade cost estimates. Caveat: the estimates come from one broker's order flow over a limited period, and many later studies using other data find impact closer to a square-root law (an exponent of 1/2) in total order size, with impact partly decaying after execution, so the exact exponent and functional form remain debated.

Kalman (1960), Journal of Basic Engineering 82(1), 35-45 (Transactions of the ASME, Series D) | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3662552 | Topics: Kalman filter

Kalman asked how to estimate the current state of a system that cannot be observed directly, such as a vehicle's position and velocity, from a stream of noisy measurements, and how to predict its future state. Earlier Wiener filtering handled such problems in the frequency domain for stationary processes and was cumbersome to compute. Kalman restated the problem in state-space form: a hidden state evolves linearly with random disturbances, x_t = F * x_(t-1) + w_t, and each observation is a linear function of the state plus noise, y_t = H * x_t + v_t. The best linear estimate can then be computed recursively, needing only the previous estimate and its uncertainty rather than the whole history. Each step predicts the state and its error covariance P, then corrects the prediction with the new observation: gain K = P * H' * (H * P * H' + R)^-1, and updated estimate = prediction + K * (observation - predicted observation), where R is the covariance of the measurement noise. When the noise is Gaussian this estimate is the best possible, not merely the best linear one. The filter guided spacecraft navigation in the Apollo programme; in finance it is used to track time-varying betas and hedge ratios, to estimate unobserved trends and to fit term-structure models. Caveat: it is optimal only for linear models with known noise covariances; misspecified noise levels degrade it, and nonlinear problems need extended, unscented or particle filters.

Harvey's book asks how to model and forecast economic time series by breaking them into components with direct interpretations, such as trend, seasonal pattern, cycle and irregular noise, each allowed to change randomly over time, rather than fitting the more abstract ARIMA models of the Box-Jenkins approach. These structural time series models are written in state-space form, so the Kalman filter delivers estimates of the unobserved components, the likelihood used to estimate the model's variances (through the prediction-error decomposition), smoothed estimates that use the full sample, and forecasts with error bands. The simplest example is the local level model: y_t = mu_t + e_t, with mu_t = mu_(t-1) + n_t, where the level mu wanders as a random walk and is observed with noise. Rule: the ratio q = variance(n) / variance(e), the signal-to-noise ratio, determines how quickly the estimated level adapts to new data; in steady state the Kalman filter for this model is equivalent to exponential smoothing with a weight set by q. The book also covers model selection, diagnostic testing, explanatory variables and interventions, and multivariate extensions, with applications to economic data. Caveat: it is a technical econometrics text; later computational and Bayesian methods, such as those in Durbin and Koopman's state-space book, broadened the toolkit; and for financial returns, which are close to unpredictable, these methods help more with tracking hidden quantities than with forecasting prices.

QUANT LIBRARY | SUMMARY in our own words (not the work's text) | "The Theory of Interest, as Determined by Impatience to Spend Income and Opportunity to Invest It" by Irving Fisher (1930), Macmillan, New York; 1st edition | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://openlibrary.org/works/OL1460746W | Topics: returns (simple, log, compounding); present value

Fisher asked what determines the rate of interest, and answered that it balances two forces: people's impatience to spend income now rather than later, and the opportunities available to invest, giving up income today for more income in the future. In his framework the value of any capital asset is the present value of the income it is expected to produce, discounted at the market rate of interest: present value = the sum over years t of income_t / (1 + r)^t, so a payment of 110 due in one year is worth 100 today at a 10 percent rate. He showed, in what is now called the Fisher separation theorem, that with a perfect capital market a firm's or person's choice of investments can be made by maximising present value, separately from preferences about when to consume, because borrowing and lending can reshape the timing of consumption. He also distinguished nominal from real interest, restating his earlier relation between interest and expected inflation: (1 + nominal rate) = (1 + real rate) * (1 + expected inflation), or approximately nominal rate ~ real rate + expected inflation. The book laid the foundations for discounted cash flow valuation and for the modern treatment of interest in economics. Caveat: real capital markets are imperfect, and borrowing and lending rates differ; empirical studies find nominal rates do not move one-for-one with expected inflation in the short run; and behavioural research shows people discount the future inconsistently rather than at one steady rate.

QUANT LIBRARY | SUMMARY in our own words (not the work's text) | "The Theory of Investment Value" by John Burr Williams (1938), Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA; 1st edition | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://openlibrary.org/works/OL1343926W | Topics: present value

Williams asked how to determine the intrinsic value of a stock or bond, as distinct from its market price, and answered with the rule of present worth: an investment is worth the present value of the cash it will pay its owners. For a stock that means dividends: value = the sum over years t of dividend_t / (1 + r)^t, where r is the investor's required rate of return. Earnings matter only insofar as they lead to dividends, since retained earnings add value only if they produce larger dividends later. He developed formulas for companies whose dividends grow at different rates in different phases, and his approach leads directly to the constant-growth formula later popularised by Myron Gordon: value = next year's dividend / (r - g), valid when the growth rate g is below r. He also stated a law of the conservation of investment value: the total value of a company does not depend on how its capitalisation is divided between bonds and stocks, an idea that anticipated the Modigliani-Miller theorem. The book, based on his doctoral thesis, made the dividend discount model the core of fundamental valuation, and Harry Markowitz has said that reading it prompted his work on portfolio selection. Caveat: values are extremely sensitive to the assumed discount and growth rates, especially when g is close to r; long-run dividend forecasts are highly uncertain; and many companies pay no dividends, so practitioners substitute free cash flows.

A graduate textbook on optimization problems whose every local optimum is also global: the objective is convex and the feasible set is convex. It teaches how to recognize and reformulate such problems (linear, quadratic, second-order cone and semidefinite programs), the duality theory that certifies an answer is optimal, and the interior-point algorithms that solve them reliably. For a quant it is the mathematics under portfolio construction. Choosing weights w to minimize portfolio variance w'Sw for a required expected return, with the weights summing to one and any linear limits on positions, is a convex quadratic program; the book uses this mean-variance problem as a worked example of a quadratic program and of a risk-return trade-off, and solving it for every required return traces the efficient frontier. Its chapters on approximation and statistical estimation treat least squares, regularized regression and maximum likelihood as convex problems, which is the fitting machinery behind regression and factor models. Rule to remember: when the objective and the constraints are convex, any local minimum is the global minimum, and the dual problem gives a bound that proves it. Caveat: the book proves how to solve a stated problem, not that the inputs are right; expected returns estimated from short histories are noisy, so optimized weights can swing wildly unless the inputs are shrunk or the weights constrained. The authors host a free PDF of the book for personal use; this library keeps only this summary.

A graduate probability textbook built on measure theory. It proves the laws of large numbers (the average of many independent draws settles on the expected value), the central limit theorem (a sum of many small independent shocks is close to normally distributed, which is why the bell curve appears so often), and then develops random walks, martingales, Markov chains, ergodic theorems and Brownian motion. A martingale is the mathematical model of a fair game: given everything known today, the expected value of tomorrow's price equals today's, which is the formal version of the random-walk view of prices. For the quant ideas here it supplies the rigorous footing for expected value, the random walk, the square-root-of-time rule, the bell curve as a limit, mean-reverting Markov processes and Monte Carlo simulation, whose averages converge because of the law of large numbers. Rule to remember: for n independent, identically distributed returns with finite variance s^2, their sum has standard deviation s * sqrt(n) and is approximately normal when n is large; averaging N simulated paths shrinks the Monte Carlo error like 1 / sqrt(N). Caveat: every theorem holds only under its assumptions, such as independence and finite variance; daily returns are fat-tailed and their volatility clusters, so the normal approximation can be poor in the tails, and the book teaches mathematics rather than market evidence. The author hosts a free PDF of the fifth edition; this library keeps only this summary.

(2009), Springer, 2nd edition (Springer Series in Statistics; the authors host a free PDF at https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/) | Licence of the work: copyright of its publisher or authors (not openly licensed); this library keeps only a summary | Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-84858-7 | Topics: backtesting; linear regression; hypothesis testing; backtest overfitting

A standard reference on statistical learning written by three Stanford statisticians. It covers linear regression and its regularized forms (ridge regression and the lasso), classification, basis expansions and splines, kernel methods, model assessment and selection, additive models and trees, boosting, neural networks, support vector machines, nearest neighbours, random forests, ensembles, unsupervised learning and problems with more variables than observations. For quant research its central lesson is honest model assessment: the error a model makes on the data it was fit to understates the error it will make on new data, so a model must be judged on data it never saw, by holding data out or by cross-validation, and searching through many models makes the best one look better than it is, which is the same trap as backtest overfitting. It also lays out least squares, the assumptions behind regression standard errors and tests, and how shrinkage trades a little bias for a large cut in variance. Rule to remember: expected prediction error = irreducible noise + bias^2 + variance; a more flexible model lowers bias and raises variance, and the best model balances the two. Caveat: most of its methods assume observations are independent; prices form a time series, so ordinary cross-validation that shuffles days lets the future leak into the past, and finance needs validation that respects time order. The authors host a free PDF of the second edition; this library keeps only this summary.
